title: Canadian novelist removed from Prix Goncourt longlist after AI allegations

reading.body:
This is a case of an AI-detection claim being used to remove a work from consideration, not a case of a system making a decision on its own. The allegation originated with an anonymous X account and a detector tool called Pangram, and the prize body acted on it after review. The failure mode here is a contested classification: a detector's output was treated as evidence that a person used AI to write a novel, and that output was then folded together with separate plagiarism allegations in earlier work.

The decision happened at the gatekeeping stage of a literary prize, before any award was made, and it extended into the author's commercial life when his Quebec publisher halted promotion. Catching this would have required the prize body to separate the detector claim from the plagiarism claim and to treat the detector result as an allegation rather than a finding. It is not established that Orélien used AI to write the novel, that the plagiarism allegations are accurate, or that the detector's output was reliable.

Orélien and his publisher Éditions Grasset have denied the allegations. A denial is not a finding either, and the reporting does not establish what evidence, if any, the Académie Goncourt reviewed beyond the allegations themselves.

reports.title: Canadian novelist removed from Prix Goncourt longlist after AI allegations

summary:
The Prix Goncourt removed Canadian author Thélyson Orélien's novel C'était ça ou mourir from its longlist after reviewing allegations that he used AI to write it. The Académie Goncourt also cited examples of alleged plagiarism in his earlier work, first reported by Montreal newspaper La Presse. The prize will be awarded in early November. Orélien and his French publisher, Éditions Grasset, have denied the allegations.

Orélien's Quebec publisher, Les Editions du Boréal, has halted promotional activities for the book, which had sold to 23 countries and was set for an English release by Scribner in 2028. Orélien, who lives in Ottawa, said he is angry and has always loved writing. The allegations began with an X account and an AI detector called Pangram.
